title: The abstract equivalence theorem
statement:
Let $(\mathcal C,F)$ be a Galois category in the sense of [def-galois-category] and
$G=\operatorname{Aut}(F)$ with the topology of [def-galois-category]. Write $\text{finite-}G\text{-}\mathbf{Sets}$ for the category whose objects are finite sets $E$ with a left action of $G$ such that the action map $G\times E\to E$ is continuous for the discrete topology on $E$, and whose morphisms are the $G$-equivariant maps. Then the functor
$\mathcal C\to \text{finite-}G\text{-}\mathbf{Sets}$, $X\mapsto F(X)$ with the induced action $\gamma\cdot x=\gamma_X(x)$, $f\mapsto F(f)$, is an equivalence of categories.

proof.text: *The functor is well defined.* Each $F(X)$ is finite by [def-galois-category](3); $G$ is a profinite group by [lem-galois-aut-profinite]; the action map $G\times F(X)\to F(X)$, $(\gamma,x)\mapsto\gamma_X(x)$, is continuous for the discrete topology on $F(X)$ by [lem-galois-action-continuous]; and for $f:X\to X'$ naturality of every $\gamma\in G$ gives $F(f)(\gamma_X(x))=\gamma_{X'}(F(f)(x))$, so $F(f)$ is $G$-equivariant. Functoriality is that of $F$.

source.place: Example 0BMW (example-from-C-F-to-G-sets) and the paragraph before Lemma 0BMR (lemma-aut-inverse-limit) in Section 0BMQ

proof.text: *Faithfulness.* $F$ is faithful by [lem-galois-axioms](1); the functor to $\text{finite-}G\text{-}\mathbf{Sets}$ has the same maps on morphisms, so it is faithful.

*Connected components go to $G$-orbits.* Let $X$ be an object and $X=\coprod_{i=1}^nX_i$ a decomposition into connected objects ([def-galois-category](2)), with coprojections $c_i:X_i\to X$. Since $F$ is exact it preserves finite coproducts, so the maps $F(c_i)$ identify $F(X)$ with the disjoint union $\bigsqcup_iF(X_i)$; each $F(c_i)$ is $G$-equivariant (step 1), so each $F(c_i)(F(X_i))$ is $G$-stable. Each $X_i$ is connected, hence not initial, so $F(X_i)\ne\emptyset$ by [lem-galois-axioms](3), and $G$ acts transitively on $F(X_i)$ by [lem-galois-transitive]. Hence the $G$-orbits of $F(X)$ are exactly the subsets $F(c_i)(F(X_i))$, $i=1,\dots,n$.

source.place: Proposition 0BN4 (proposition-galois), proof, first paragraph: 'Hence for general X the functor F sends the connected components of X ... to the G-orbits of F(X)'

proof.text: *$G$-stable subsets come from unions of components.* With the notation of step 3, let $S\subseteq F(X)$ be $G$-stable. Then $S$ is a union of orbits, so by step 3 there is $I\subseteq\{1,\dots,n\}$ with $S=\bigcup_{i\in I}F(c_i)(F(X_i))$. Let $Z=\coprod_{i\in I}X_i$ (a finite coproduct, [def-galois-category](1)) and $j:Z\to X$ the map with components $c_i$, $i\in I$. As $F$ preserves finite coproducts, $F(j)$ is the inclusion of $\bigsqcup_{i\in I}F(X_i)$ into $\bigsqcup_iF(X_i)=F(X)$; it is injective with image $S$, so $j$ is a monomorphism by [lem-galois-axioms](2) and $F(j)$ identifies $F(Z)$ with $S$.

source.place: Proposition 0BN4 (proposition-galois), proof, first paragraph: 'Hence there exists a union of connected components Z of X x Y, which comes equipped with a monomorphism Z -> X x Y, with F(Z) = Gamma_s'

proof.text: *Fullness.* Let $s:F(X)\to F(Y)$ be $G$-equivariant. Since $F$ preserves finite products, $(F(\mathrm{pr}_1),F(\mathrm{pr}_2)):F(X\times Y)\to F(X)\times F(Y)$ is a bijection, $G$-equivariant for the diagonal action (step 1). The graph $\Gamma_s=\{(x,s(x))\}$ is stable under the diagonal action because $s$ is equivariant; by step 4 applied to $X\times Y$ there is a monomorphism $j:Z\to X\times Y$ with $F(j)(F(Z))$ corresponding to $\Gamma_s$. The map $F(\mathrm{pr}_1\circ j):F(Z)\to F(X)$ is the bijection $\Gamma_s\to F(X)$, $(x,s(x))\mapsto x$, so $p=\mathrm{pr}_1\circ j$ is an isomorphism because $F$ reflects isomorphisms ([def-galois-category](4)). Put $f=\mathrm{pr}_2\circ j\circ p^{-1}:X\to Y$; then $F(f)(x)=s(x)$ for every $x\in F(X)$. With step 2 the functor is fully faithful.

source.place: Proposition 0BN4 (proposition-galois), proof, first paragraph: 'Let X and Y be objects and let s : F(X) -> F(Y) be a map ... Hence F is fully faithful'

proof.text: *Reduction of essential surjectivity to $G/H$.* Let $E$ be a finite $G$-set. It is the disjoint union of its finitely many orbits. For $e\in E$ the stabilizer $H=\{g:ge=e\}$ is the preimage of $\{e\}$ under the continuous map $g\mapsto ge$ to the discrete set $E$, hence open, and $Ge\cong G/H$, $gH\mapsto ge$, as $G$-sets, so $H$ has finite index. If for each orbit $G/H_k$ ($k=1,\dots,m$) there is $X_k$ with $F(X_k)\cong G/H_k$ as $G$-sets, then $F(\coprod_kX_k)\cong\bigsqcup_kF(X_k)\cong E$ as $G$-sets, because $F$ preserves finite coproducts ([def-galois-category](1),(4)) and the coprojections are equivariant. So it suffices to realize $G/H$ for every open subgroup $H\subseteq G$ of finite index.

source.place: Proposition 0BN4 (proposition-galois), proof, second paragraph, first two sentences

proof.text: *Finitely many connected objects controlling $H$.* Let $H\subseteq G$ be an open subgroup of finite index. The topology of $G$ is induced from $\prod_X\operatorname{Aut}(F(X))$ with the discrete factors ([def-galois-category]), so the open neighbourhood $H$ of $1$ contains a basic one: there are finitely many objects $X'_1,\dots,X'_r$ with $K'=\{\gamma\in G:\gamma_{X'_l}=\mathrm{id}\ \forall l\}=\ker\bigl(G\to\prod_l\operatorname{Aut}(F(X'_l))\bigr)\subseteq H$. Decompose each $X'_l$ into connected objects ([def-galois-category](2)) and let $X_1,\dots,X_t$ be all components so obtained. By step 3, $F(X'_l)$ is the union of the images of the $F$ of its components under equivariant injections, so $\gamma$ acts trivially on $F(X'_l)$ as soon as it acts trivially on each $F$ of its components. Hence $K=\ker\bigl(G\to\prod_{i}\operatorname{Aut}(F(X_i))\bigr)\subseteq K'\subseteq H$ with all $X_i$ connected. If $t=0$ then $K=G=H$ and $G/H$ is $F$ of a final object by [lem-galois-axioms](3); assume $t\ge1$.

source.place: Proposition 0BN4 (proposition-galois), proof, second paragraph: 'By definition of the topology on G there exists a finite collection of objects X_i ... We may assume X_i is connected for all i'

proof.text: *A Galois object dominating the $X_i$.* Let $P=X_1\times\dots\times X_t$ (finite limit, [def-galois-category](1)); $F(P)=\prod_iF(X_i)$ is nonempty since each $F(X_i)\neq\emptyset$ ([lem-galois-axioms](3)). Of a decomposition of $P$ into connected objects ([def-galois-category](2)) pick a component $P_0$; it maps to $P$ by its coprojection. By [lem-galois-object-exists] there is a Galois object $Y$ (in the sense of [lem-galois-axioms](6)) and a morphism $Y\to P_0$. For each $i$ the composite $q_i:Y\to P_0\to P\to X_i$ is a morphism between connected objects, hence an epimorphism ([lem-galois-axioms](4)), so $F(q_i):F(Y)\to F(X_i)$ is surjective ([lem-galois-axioms](2)) and $G$-equivariant (step 1).

source.place: Proposition 0BN4 (proposition-galois), proof, second paragraph: 'We can choose a Galois object Y mapping to a connected component of prod X_i using Lemma 0BN2' and 'Since F(Y) surjects onto F(X_i)'

proof.text: *$F(Y)\cong G/U$ with $U$ open normal.* Fix $y\in F(Y)$. $G$ acts transitively on $F(Y)$ by [lem-galois-transitive] ($Y$ is connected), so $F(Y)\cong G/U$, $gU\mapsto gy$, with $U$ the stabilizer of $y$, open by [lem-galois-action-continuous] (as in step 6). $Y$ is Galois, so $\operatorname{Aut}(Y)$ acts transitively on $F(Y)$ ([lem-galois-axioms](6)), and each $F(a)$, $a\in\operatorname{Aut}(Y)$, is $G$-equivariant (step 1). Given $g\in G$ choose $a$ with $F(a)(y)=gy$; for $u\in U$, $ugy=uF(a)(y)=F(a)(uy)=F(a)(y)=gy$, so $g^{-1}ug\in U$. Hence $U$ is normal.

source.place: Proposition 0BN4 (proposition-galois), proof, second paragraph: 'Choose an isomorphism F(Y) = G/U ... This implies that U is normal'

proof.text: *$U\subseteq H$.* For $u\in U$ and any point $gy$ of $F(Y)$, $u\,gy=g(g^{-1}ug)y=gy$ by normality (step 9), so $U$ acts trivially on $F(Y)$. As $F(q_i):F(Y)\to F(X_i)$ is surjective and equivariant (step 8), $U$ acts trivially on every $F(X_i)$, i.e. $U\subseteq K\subseteq H$ (step 7).

source.place: Proposition 0BN4 (proposition-galois), proof, second paragraph: 'Since F(Y) surjects onto F(X_i) for each i we see that U subset H'

proof.text: *$\operatorname{Aut}(Y)\cong(G/U)^{\mathrm{op}}$.* By steps 2 and 5, $a\mapsto F(a)$ is a bijection $\operatorname{Aut}(Y)\to\operatorname{Aut}_G(F(Y))=\operatorname{Aut}_G(G/U)$ compatible with composition. A $G$-equivariant $\varphi:G/U\to G/U$ is determined by $\varphi(U)=nU$, and then $\varphi(gU)=gnU$; conversely, $U$ being normal, $R_n:gU\mapsto gnU$ is well defined and equivariant for every $n$, and $R_n\circ R_m=R_{mn}$, $R_n=\mathrm{id}$ iff $n\in U$. So $n U\mapsto R_n$ is an isomorphism $(G/U)^{\mathrm{op}}\to\operatorname{Aut}_G(G/U)$. Let $M\subseteq\operatorname{Aut}(Y)$ be the subgroup corresponding to $(H/U)^{\mathrm{op}}$ ($H\supseteq U$ by step 10); it is finite, of order $[H:U]$.

source.place: Proposition 0BN4 (proposition-galois), proof, second paragraph: 'Let M subset Aut(Y) be the finite subgroup corresponding to (H/U)^opp subset (G/U)^opp = Aut_{G-Sets}(G/U) = Aut(Y)'

proof.text: *$X=Y/M$ realizes $G/H$.* Let $X$ be the colimit of the diagram $M\to\mathcal C$ given by the action of the finite group $M$ on $Y$, i.e. the coequalizer of the finite family of arrows $m:Y\to Y$, $m\in M$, with map $\pi:Y\to X$; it exists because it is a finite colimit ([def-galois-category](1)). $F$ is exact ([def-galois-category](4)), so $F(\pi)$ identifies $F(X)$ with the quotient of $F(Y)$ by the equivalence relation generated by $z\sim F(m)(z)$, which is the orbit relation of the group $M$; and $F(\pi)$ is $G$-equivariant (step 1), so the bijection is one of $G$-sets for the action induced on the quotient. Under $F(Y)\cong G/U$ the action of $m\in M$ is $R_n$ for $nU\in H/U$ (step 11), and the $M$-orbit of $gU$ is $\{ghU:h\in H\}$, i.e. corresponds to $gH$. Hence $F(X)\cong(G/U)/(H/U)\cong G/H$ as $G$-sets, and with step 6 the functor is essentially surjective, so (with steps 2 and 5) an equivalence.

source.place: Proposition 0BN4 (proposition-galois), proof, second paragraph, last two sentences: 'Set X = Y/M ... Since F is exact we see that F(X) = G/H'
